title: Disproof type is not ¬ (reference statement)
explanation: The `not_…` theorem was found, but its type is not syntactically `¬ S` for the reference type `S`. In the logs the usual cause was a universe mismatch: the reference uses `Type*` (elaborated as `Type u_1`), while the disproof wrote `Type u` or a fresh `Type*` inside the negation.
fixes: Copy the reference statement verbatim inside `¬ ( … )`, turning the theorem's binders into `∀` binders, in the same order and with the same implicitness and instance arguments.

Match universe names: write `Type u_1` (declare `universe u_1`) where the reference has `Type*`, and instantiate the counterexample at that level, e.g. `G.{u_1}` or `ULift.{u_1} (Fin n)`. This fixed the rejected submissions in the logs.
Keep inline proof terms such as `(by simp)` inside the statement exactly as in the reference.
example: X.not_conj must have type ¬ (reference statement)

pattern: declarations the statement depends on were changed or are missing
title: Definitions or auxiliary proofs of the statement differ
explanation: The checker compares every constant the target's statement uses. A name ending in `._proof_1` is the auxiliary proof Lean extracts from a `by …` term inside the statement (e.g. `Finset.max' (by simp)`). It changes when the surrounding statement text, universes or instances change.
fixes: Do not redefine or copy the challenge's definitions; use the ones in the challenge file unchanged.
If the listed name ends in `_proof_N`, the statement around an inline `by` differs from the reference (often the universe level). Restore the exact reference text.
Never edit the statement to make the proof easier; prove a helper lemma instead and apply it.
example: declarations the statement depends on were changed or are missing: Ns.thm._proof_1

title: Target (or not_ target) missing
explanation: The checker did not find the expected declaration name. For a disproof the name is the reference name with its last component prefixed by `not_`, in the same namespace (for `A.b.parts.i` it is `A.b.parts.not_i`).
fixes: Rename the theorem to the exact expected name. The rejection message spells it out.
Check that it is not inside an extra `namespace`/`section` with a name, and that it is not `private`.
For a proof, keep the reference theorem's name and replace only its `sorry`.
example: Ns.thm.parts.not_i not found in the submission

title: Statement differs from the reference
explanation: The type of your target theorem is not identical (after elaboration) to the reference type. Harmless-looking edits such as renaming a bound variable are fine, but changing binders, coercions, `≤` vs `<`, instance arguments or universes is not.
fixes: Start from the challenge file and replace only the `sorry` of the target.
If you need a different but equivalent form, prove it as a separate lemma and close the target with `exact (my_lemma …)` or `simpa using …`.
Partial proofs are checked the same way: open lemmas may change, the target statement may not.
example: statement differs from the reference

pattern: failed to synthesize(?: instance of type class)?\s+(?:Insert|Singleton|Union|Inter|SDiff|DecidableEq)\b
title: Finset literal or operation needs DecidableEq
explanation: `{u, v} : Finset α`, `insert`, `∪`, `∩` and `\` on finsets need `DecidableEq α`. Without it Lean cannot build the `Insert` instance, and `{u, v}` may also be tried as structure-instance notation ("`u` is not a field of structure `Finset`"). The failure then shows up later as goals mentioning `sorry`.
fixes: Add `classical` at the start of the proof, or add `[DecidableEq α]` to the lemma's binders, if the statement allows it.
Annotate the literal: `({u, v} : Finset α)`. Or use a `Set` (`({u, v} : Set α)`) when decidability is not needed.
Fix this first: the later errors with goals that mention `sorry` follow from it.
example: failed to synthesize instance of type class Insert α (Finset α)

title: Import not allowed
explanation: nosorry accepts imports only from Mathlib, Batteries, Aesop, Qq, Plausible, ProofWidgets, Init, Std, FormalConjectures*, Physlib and QuantumInfo. SciLean and PhyslibAlpha are refused on purpose. A module name that is malformed or truncated is also reported this way.
fixes: Remove the import and inline the definitions or lemmas you need into the solution file.
To import another numbered formal-conjectures problem, quote the numeric component: `import FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«28»`.
Use `import Mathlib` (or the specific Mathlib modules) rather than a third-party package.
example: import not allowed: Foo.Bar

title: native_decide is not accepted
explanation: `native_decide`, `decide +native` and `Lean.ofReduceBool` trust compiled code, and nosorry accepts only `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice`. This was the most frequent preflight rejection in the logs. A `native_decide` that is literally present in the reference statement is tolerated as long as your target does not depend on it.
fixes: Replace it by `decide +kernel` (kernel evaluation, no compiler), or by `decide` on smaller pieces.
Split a big computation into named lemmas over small ranges, each closed by `decide +kernel` or `norm_num`, and combine them with `rw`/`simp`.
For number theory, prove facts structurally (multiplicativity, `norm_num` primality) instead of evaluating huge numbers.
example: `native_decide` trusts the compiler and is not accepted

pattern: The rfl tactic failed|Tactic .rfl. failed|is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side
title: rfl failed: sides are not definitionally equal
explanation: `rfl` needs the two sides to be equal by unfolding definitions. Linear maps and equivalences built by tactics (`LinearEquiv.ofFinrankEq`, `Classical.choice`-based constructions), well-founded recursion and `irreducible` definitions do not unfold to the value you expect.
fixes: Prove the equation by its defining lemma: `simp [myFun]`, `rw [myFun_apply]`, or `ext` followed by `simp`.
If the map comes from an existence theorem, keep the property you need (`hE : ∀ x, E x = …`) when you construct it, instead of hoping it unfolds.
Try `decide` for decidable closed goals, `norm_num` for numerals, `ring` for commutative-ring identities.
example: Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side f (z, h) is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side ((0, z), h)

pattern: reference does not compile|unknown module prefix
title: Reference statement does not compile (infrastructure)
explanation: The challenge file itself failed to build on the verifier, for example "unknown module prefix 'FormalConjecturesUtil'" when the build environment lacked a library. This is not a fault in your proof.
fixes: Resubmit later or report it to the maintainers. Do not change the imports of the challenge file to work around it.
If you are submitting a formalization, check that the file compiles locally with the same toolchain (Lean v4.33.1) and imports only allowed modules.
example: reference does not compile: error: unknown module prefix 'Foo'

title: Statement checker crashed (infrastructure)
explanation: The statement/axiom checker produced no readable verdict, usually because it ran out of time or memory on a very large environment. It is a verifier-side error, not a rejection of the proof.
fixes: Resubmit. If it repeats, report it, mentioning the submission size.
Very large files (hundreds of thousands of characters) are more likely to hit this. Removing unused helper code helps.
example: checker output unreadable:

pattern: verifier run failed|the run stopped before producing a result|HTTP 401
title: Remote verifier run failed (infrastructure)
explanation: Large or repository submissions are checked on a remote runner. The run was interrupted or could not be read, so there is no verdict yet.
fixes: Resubmit later. The submission was not rejected on its merits.
Report it if it repeats for the same submission.
example: verifier run failed: the run stopped before producing a result

title: Linter: let preferred over letI (warning)
explanation: A style warning, not an error: in a proof (a Prop goal) `letI`/`haveI` are unnecessary. It can flood the compiler output and hide the real error.
fixes: Ignore it while hunting the error: search the output for `error:`.
Replace `letI`/`haveI` by `let`/`have` inside proofs, or add `set_option linter.style.haveILetI false` (allowed by nosorry).
example: warning: The goal is a proposition, so `let` is preferred over `letI`.

title: Linter: unused simp argument (warning)
explanation: A warning that a lemma passed to `simp`/`simp only` was not used. Harmless, but the noise can bury real errors.
fixes: Remove the listed argument, or silence the linter with `set_option linter.unusedSimpArgs false`.
Look for lines with `error:` to find what actually failed.
example: warning: This simp argument is unused: Foo.bar

title: Declaration uses sorry
explanation: A warning that a declaration still contains `sorry` (or `admit`). nosorry accepts it only in declarations the target does not depend on, or in a partial proof whose open lemmas are shared.
fixes: Find which `sorry` your target depends on. The verdict lists them as open lemmas.
For a complete proof, remove every `sorry` on which the target depends. Otherwise submit as `partial` with shared lemmas.
Other theorems of the challenge file may keep their `sorry`.
example: warning: declaration uses `sorry`

pattern: the target theorem itself still uses sorry
title: Target theorem still uses sorry
explanation: The theorem you are proving still contains `sorry` directly, so this is neither a proof nor a partial proof.
fixes: Replace the target's `sorry` by a proof. If you can only reduce it to lemmas, state them as separate theorems with `sorry` and submit as `partial`.
example: the target theorem itself still uses sorry

pattern: the proof still depends on sorry
title: Proof depends on sorry: submit as partial
explanation: Your target is sorry-free, but some lemma it uses (listed) still has `sorry`. Proofs and disproofs must be complete.
fixes: Prove the listed lemmas, or resubmit with kind `partial` (ideally with shared lemmas so others can prove them).
Check for a forgotten `sorry` in a helper's `have` or in a `decreasing_by` block.
example: the proof still depends on sorry (Ns.helper) — submit it as a partial proof instead

title: Non-standard axioms
explanation: `#print axioms` of the target shows something beyond `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice`, typically `Lean.ofReduceBool` (from `native_decide`), or an axiom declared in a dependency.
fixes: Remove `native_decide`/`decide +native` and use `decide +kernel` or a structural proof.
Do not declare `axiom`s. State the fact as a theorem (with `sorry`, as a partial proof) instead.
example: non-standard axioms: Lean.ofReduceBool

title: axiom declarations refused
explanation: The preflight found an `axiom` command. Axioms would let anything be proved.
fixes: Turn the axiom into a `theorem … := by sorry` and submit as `partial` with shared lemmas, so the step becomes a lemma problem.
example: new axioms are not allowed

pattern: (unsafe. / .partial. definitions|implemented_by. / .extern|.opaque. declarations|initializers) are not allowed|meta-level attributes are not allowed
title: unsafe / partial / extern / opaque refused
explanation: Constructs that bypass the kernel or hide definitions (`unsafe`, `partial def`, `implemented_by`, `extern`, `opaque`, `initialize`, `@[csimp]` and similar attributes) are refused.
fixes: Write a total definition: structural recursion, or `termination_by` with a `decreasing_by` proof, or `Nat.rec`/`Nat.iterate`.
Use `def` (or `noncomputable def`) instead of `opaque`; `irreducible_def` is fine if you need opacity for performance.
example: `unsafe` / `partial` definitions are not allowed

pattern: evaluation / debugging commands are not allowed
title: #eval / #print / #check refused
explanation: `#eval`, `#print`, `#check`, `#reduce`, `#synth`, `#exit`, `run_cmd` and similar commands are refused in submissions, including `#print axioms` lines copied from ported code.
fixes: Delete these lines before submitting. Use them only locally.
example: evaluation / debugging commands are not allowed

title: exact? / apply? / hint / #loogle refused
explanation: Search tactics and commands (`exact?`, `apply?`, `rw?`, `hint`, `#leansearch`, `#loogle`, `#moogle`) must be replaced by what they found. The rule also fires on a hypothesis named `hint` used at the start of a tactic line.
fixes: Run `exact?` locally, then paste the suggested `exact foo …` term.
Rename hypotheses called `hint` (e.g. to `hInt`).
example: search commands (#leansearch, #loogle, exact?…) must be replaced by the lemmas they found before submitting

pattern: custom syntax / elaborators are not allowed|meta-programming API is not allowed
title: Custom syntax / metaprogramming refused
explanation: `macro`, `syntax`, `notation`, `elab`, `infix` and `import Lean`/`Lean.Elab`/`Lean.Meta` are refused in solutions. Notation that already appears verbatim in the reference statement is tolerated.
fixes: Replace notation by plain definitions or `abbrev`s, and macros by repeated tactic blocks or `all_goals`/`<;>`.
If you need a local `open … in`, that is fine; it is not custom syntax.
example: custom syntax / elaborators are not allowed in solutions

title: set_option not allowed
explanation: Only `maxHeartbeats` and `synthInstance.maxHeartbeats` up to 9,999,999, `maxRecDepth` up to 99,999, `linter.*`, `autoImplicit`/`relaxedAutoImplicit` and `pp.*` are accepted. Values of 10,000,000 heartbeats or 100,000 recursion depth are refused, as is any other option.
fixes: Lower the value (e.g. `set_option maxRecDepth 99999`), and scope it with `set_option … in` before a single declaration.
Remove options like `trace.*`, `maxSynthPendingDepth` or `backward.*`; restructure the proof instead.
example: only maxHeartbeats (≤ 9,999,999), maxRecDepth, synthInstance.maxHeartbeats, linter.*, autoImplicit and pp.* options are allowed

title: IO refused
explanation: Any mention of `IO`, `EIO`, `BaseIO` or `System.*` is refused, even in a definition that is never run.
fixes: Remove the code. Proofs never need IO. If a name merely contains the token `IO`, rename it.
example: IO is not allowed

pattern: must be a theorem|target is not a theorem
title: Target is not a theorem
explanation: The target was declared with `def`, `abbrev` or `instance` (or it is missing and a definition with the same name exists).
fixes: Declare it with `theorem` (or `lemma`) under the exact reference name.
example: target is not a theorem

title: Compilation timed out
explanation: The whole file took longer than the verifier's wall-clock limit. Heartbeat limits are per declaration; this one is for the whole build.
fixes: Profile locally and speed up the slowest declarations: `simp only [...]` instead of `simp`, `nlinarith only [...]`, smaller `decide` chunks.
Delete unused helper lemmas, especially heavy computations.
example: compilation timed out

title: Kernel replay failed
explanation: The compiled module was re-checked by `leanchecker` and a declaration failed. Usually this is a kernel-only limit (deep recursion, a definitional unfolding the elaborator accepted lazily), and rarely a genuine soundness issue.
fixes: Look for `decide`/`rfl` proofs on large terms. Replace them with `decide +kernel` on smaller pieces, or with structural lemmas.
Check that the file compiles locally with `lake env lean` and replays with `leanchecker`.
example: kernel replay failed: (kernel) deep recursion detected

title: Comparator rejected
explanation: The independent comparator (leanprover/comparator) found a difference in the theorem, its definitions or its axioms relative to the reference.
fixes: Treat it like a statement mismatch: restore the exact reference statement and definitions, and remove non-standard axioms.
example: comparator rejected:

title: Duplicate of an earlier submission
explanation: After removing comments, whitespace and declaration names, your source is identical to another user's earlier submission on this problem.
fixes: Do not resubmit someone else's proof. Build on it (cite it) or find a different argument. Another proof of a settled problem earns nothing.
example: identical to earlier submission s-… on this problem

title: Reference contains sorry outside an answer(...) slot
explanation: The reference type itself contains a `sorry` that is not an `answer(...)` hole. The statement is incomplete and cannot be proved as stated.
fixes: Report it as a critique of the statement instead of submitting a proof.
example: the reference type contains sorry outside an answer(...) slot; report it as a critique

pattern: must be stated with sorry as its proof|the statement introduces axioms
title: Formalization must be a sorry'd statement
explanation: A formalization submission states a problem: its target must be a theorem whose proof is `sorry`, and it must not add axioms.
fixes: Write `theorem name : statement := by sorry`, and keep auxiliary definitions sorry-free and axiom-free.
Sanity checks with `native_decide` are not accepted in formalizations either; use `decide` or `decide +kernel`.
example: Ns.thm must be stated with sorry as its proof: a formalization is a problem, not a proof

title: Unknown identifier
explanation: The name does not exist in scope. Common causes: a Mathlib rename (lemma names drift between versions), a missing `open`, a Lean 3 name, or a typo in a local hypothesis.
fixes: Search for the current name: try the obvious modern spelling (`Nat.lt_irrefl` → `lt_irrefl`, `_iff` variants, `Finset.card_le_of_subset` → `Finset.card_le_card`), or use `exact?` locally.
Add the namespace (`Nat.`, `Finset.`, `SimpleGraph.`) or an `open … in`.
Check `autoImplicit`: with it off, unbound lowercase names in signatures are errors.
example: unknown identifier 'foo_bar'

title: Unknown constant
explanation: A fully qualified name (in `rw`, `simp`, `@foo` or the dot notation) does not exist, typically after a Mathlib rename or deprecation removal.
fixes: Find the replacement: deprecated aliases name their successor in the warning of the previous version, and Mathlib usually keeps the same statement under a new name (`dite_eq_left` → `dif_pos`).
Add a local shim lemma with the old name proved by the new one when porting large files.
example: unknown constant 'Nat.foo_bar'

title: Failed to synthesize instance
explanation: Type class resolution could not find an instance: decidability (`Decidable`, `DecidableEq`, `DecidablePred`), finiteness (`Fintype`, `Finite`), an algebraic structure, or a coercion that does not exist.
fixes: For decidability, add `classical` at the start of the tactic proof, or `open Classical in` before a definition.
For `Fintype` of a subtype or set, use `Set.toFinite`/`Fintype.ofFinite`, or state the lemma with `[Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]`.
Check the types: `HAdd ℕ ℝ ?` or `HDiv ℕ ℕ ℝ` means a missing cast; write `(n : ℝ)`.
example: failed to synthesize Fintype ↑s

pattern: failed to synthesize(?: instance of type class)?\s+OfNat
title: Numeral on a type without numerals
explanation: A literal such as `2` was elaborated at a type that has no `OfNat` instance (a `Prop`, a `Set`, a function type), usually because of a wrong argument order or missing parentheses.
fixes: Add a type ascription `(2 : ℕ)` and check the expected type of the argument.
Check operator precedence: `f 2 ^ k` is `(f 2) ^ k`.
example: failed to synthesize OfNat (Set ℕ) 2

title: Typeclass instance problem is stuck
explanation: Lean cannot even start instance search because a type is still a metavariable, typically a numeral or a lambda whose type is not determined.
fixes: Add type ascriptions: `(0 : ℝ)`, `(fun n : ℕ => …)`, or give explicit arguments with `(α := ℕ)`.
example: typeclass instance problem is stuck, it is often due to metavariables

title: Type mismatch (often a coercion ℕ → ℤ → ℝ)
explanation: The term has a different type than expected. With numbers this is usually a coercion problem: `↑(a + b)` vs `↑a + ↑b`, `((n : ℤ) : ℝ)` vs `(n : ℝ)`, or ℕ subtraction/division that does not commute with casts.
fixes: Normalise casts with `push_cast`, `norm_cast`, `exact_mod_cast h` or `simpa using h`.
For `↑(n - k)` give `Nat.cast_sub hk` (needs `k ≤ n`); for `↑(n / k)` use `Nat.cast_div` (needs divisibility) or avoid it.
Use `zify`/`qify`/`rify` with the needed `≤` facts to move a whole goal to ℤ/ℚ/ℝ.
example: type mismatch: h has type ↑(a + b) ≤ ↑c but is expected to have type ↑a + ↑b ≤ ↑c

title: Application type mismatch
explanation: An argument passed to a function or lemma has the wrong type, often because the arguments are in the wrong order, an implicit argument was made explicit, or a hypothesis is stated with `<` where `≤` is expected.
fixes: Check the lemma's signature (hover, or `#check` locally) and pass named arguments: `foo (n := 3) (h := hk)`.
Convert the hypothesis first: `hk.le`, `Nat.lt_succ_iff.mp hk`, `by omega`.
Use `convert foo … using 2` to see exactly which parts differ.
example: application type mismatch: foo h argument h has type a < b but is expected to have type a ≤ b

title: Motive is not type correct (rw)
explanation: `rw` abstracted the term you are rewriting, but some other part of the goal (a proof term, a dependent type such as `Fin n`, or a `Finset.max' s h`) depends on it, so the result does not typecheck.
fixes: Use `simp only [h]` or `simp_rw [h]`, which can rewrite under binders and handle dependencies better.
Generalise first: `generalize hx : f n = x at *`, or `subst` if `h : x = t` with `x` a variable.
Use `Fin.cast`/`congr`/`convert` for dependent types, or prove the statement for a general `n` and specialise.
example: motive is not type correct

pattern: maximum recursion depth has been reached
title: Maximum recursion depth reached
explanation: Elaboration recursed too deeply, typically in `decide`, `rfl` or `simp` evaluating a large term, or in `whnf` on big numerals or long lists.
fixes: Replace `decide` by `decide +kernel`, which skips the elaborator's evaluation and lets the kernel check the instance.
Split the computation into smaller lemmas, or prove it structurally (`norm_num`, `simp` with recursion equations).
As a last resort `set_option maxRecDepth 99999 in` (nosorry's maximum).
example: maximum recursion depth has been reached; use `set_option maxRecDepth <num>` to increase limit

title: Deterministic timeout (maxHeartbeats)
explanation: A declaration used more than its heartbeat budget (200000 by default). Typical culprits are unrestricted `simp`, `nlinarith`/`polyrith` with many hypotheses, `decide` on large structures and expensive instance search.
fixes: Locate the slow tactic (comment out parts, or use `set_option profiler true` locally).
Use `simp only [...]`, `nlinarith only [...]`, `norm_num [specific lemmas]`. Split the proof into lemmas.
If it is just big, `set_option maxHeartbeats 1600000 in` before that declaration (≤ 9,999,999 on nosorry).
example: (deterministic) timeout at `whnf`, maximum number of heartbeats (200000) has been reached

title: linarith / nlinarith failed
explanation: `linarith` found no linear combination of the hypotheses that proves the goal. `nlinarith` reports the same message when its products of hypotheses are not enough. Common causes: the needed fact is nonlinear, lives behind a cast, or is not in the context.
fixes: Add the missing facts explicitly: `linarith [h1, sq_nonneg (a - b), mul_pos ha hb]`.
For nonlinear goals, give `nlinarith` the exact products: `nlinarith [mul_nonneg ha hb, sq_nonneg (x - 1)]`.
Normalise casts first (`push_cast at *`), and for ℕ goals with subtraction prefer `omega`.
example: linarith failed to find a contradiction

pattern: omega could not prove the goal
title: omega could not prove the goal
explanation: `omega` handles linear arithmetic over ℕ and ℤ with `+`, `*` by constants, `/` and `%` by numerals, and truncated subtraction. It fails on products of variables, on `^`, or when the fact it needs is hidden inside a definition.
fixes: Bring the needed facts into the context as hypotheses (`have := Nat.mul_le_mul …`) and name nonlinear subterms (`set m := a * b with hm`).
Unfold definitions first (`simp only [f] at *` or `unfold f`), since omega does not see through them.
For real or rational goals use `linarith`; for nonlinear ones `nlinarith` or `positivity`.
example: omega could not prove the goal: a possible counterexample may satisfy the constraints

title: simp made no progress
explanation: None of the simp lemmas applied. The term is probably not in the syntactic form the lemmas expect (hidden behind a definition, a coercion, or a different but equal expression).
fixes: Unfold the definition explicitly: `simp [myDef]` or `unfold myDef`.
Check the goal with the infoview; use `rw` with the exact lemma, or `simp only [...]` with the right lemma names.
Remove the `simp` if the goal is already in the form you want; `simp at h` failing can also mean `h` is unchanged.
example: simp made no progress

title: Unsolved goals
explanation: The tactic block ended while goals remained. Often a case split (`rcases`, `interval_cases`, `constructor`, `induction`) produced more goals than the following tactics handled, or a `<;>` combinator closed only some of them.
fixes: Read the listed goals: handle each case with `·` bullets, or close them uniformly with `all_goals …` or `<;>`.
If a goal mentions `sorry` or `?m`, an earlier elaboration error is the real cause; fix that first.
example:
unsolved goals
case h
⊢ 0 < n

pattern: failed to reduce to (true|false)|did not reduce to .?isTrue|decide failed|failed to synthesize\s+Decidable
title: decide failed to reduce
explanation: `decide` could not evaluate the `Decidable` instance to `isTrue`. Either the proposition is false, the instance is not computable (classical, `Real`, `Set` membership, `Nat.find`, well-founded recursion), or evaluation got stuck on an opaque definition.
fixes: Check the statement is actually true for the concrete values.
Try `decide +kernel` when evaluation is merely too slow for the elaborator.

Make the instance computable: state it over `Finset`/`Fin`/`Bool` data, provide `DecidablePred`/`DecidableRel` instances, or unfold to structural recursion. `native_decide` is not accepted on nosorry.
example: decide failed to reduce to true/false

pattern: consider marking it as .noncomputable.|failed to compile definition
title: Definition must be noncomputable
explanation: The definition uses something without executable code (`Classical.choice`, `Real` operations, `sInf`, `Nat.find` on a classical predicate), so it cannot be compiled.
fixes: Mark it `noncomputable def`, or put `noncomputable section` at the top of the file.
If you need to compute with it (`decide`), redefine it computably and prove it equal to the noncomputable version.
example: failed to compile definition, consider marking it as 'noncomputable' because it depends on 'Real.sqrt'

pattern: universe level|stuck at solving universe constraint|invalid universe
title: Universe level problems
explanation: Lean cannot reconcile universe levels: a lemma quantified over `Type u` is applied to a type in another universe, or a statement uses `Type*` and your proof introduces a different universe name.
fixes: Name universes explicitly (`universe u_1`, `{α : Type u_1}`) to match the reference, and instantiate constants with `.{u_1}`.
Lift concrete types to the right universe with `ULift.{u_1} (Fin n)`.
Avoid `Sort*`/`Type*` in helper lemmas that must line up with a given statement.
example: stuck at solving universe constraint max (u_1+1) ?u =?= u+1

pattern: don't know how to synthesize (placeholder|implicit argument)
title: Cannot synthesize placeholder
explanation: A `_` or an implicit argument could not be inferred from the context, often because the expected type is unknown at that point (e.g. in a `have` without a type, or `Finset.sum_le_sum _`).
fixes: Give the type: `have h : T := …`, or pass the argument explicitly with `(x := …)` or `@foo _ _ x`.
Use `refine foo ?_ ?_` to leave real subgoals instead of `_`.
example: don't know how to synthesize placeholder for argument 'f'

pattern: invalid field( notation)?\b|is not a field of structure
title: Invalid field notation
explanation: `h.foo` was used, but no `T.foo` exists for the head type `T` of `h`, typically because `h` is a `Prop` with a different head symbol than you think (`¬`, `↔`, `≤` unfolding), or because the lemma lives in another namespace.
fixes: Call the lemma by its full name: `Nat.le_of_lt_succ h` instead of `h.le_of_lt_succ`.
Check the head of the type: for `h : a ∈ s` with `s : Finset α`, the namespace is `Finset.Mem`/`Finset`, not `Set`.
`{u, v}` being read as a structure instance ("is not a field of structure") means the `Insert` instance is missing; see the DecidableEq hint.
example: invalid field 'foo', the environment does not contain 'Nat.foo'

title: Ambiguous notation or name
explanation: Two opened namespaces provide the same name or notation (e.g. `Finset.card` and `Set.card` as `#`, `Nat.sub` lemmas in root and `Nat`, `π` from `Real` and `Nat.Prime` counting).
fixes: Use the fully qualified name (`Finset.sum_comm`, `_root_.foo`).
Narrow the `open`: `open Finset in` only where needed, or remove a conflicting `open`.
example: ambiguous, possible interpretations: _root_.foo, Nat.foo

title: Unexpected token (often Lean 3 syntax)
explanation: The parser hit syntax it does not understand. Typical sources are Lean 3 / mathlib3 idioms: `begin … end`, `λ x, e`, `assume`, `from`, `at h ⊢` written oddly, `{ }` blocks for goals, `cases h with x hx`, or `$`.
fixes: Translate to Lean 4: `by` + indentation instead of `begin … end`, `fun x => e` (or `fun x ↦ e`), `intro` instead of `assume`, `obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := h` instead of `cases h with x hx`, `<|` instead of `$`.
Use `·` bullets for subgoals and `;`/newline between tactics; check for a missing `:=` or `by`.
example: unexpected token ','; expected '↦', '=>'

title: Kernel deep recursion
explanation: The kernel ran out of stack while type-checking, usually in a `decide`/`rfl` proof that unfolds a large computation, or in a huge term from `simp` on big numerals.
fixes: Split the computation into many small `decide +kernel` lemmas and combine them with `rw`.
Use binary-friendly representations and `norm_num` for arithmetic on large numbers instead of unary unfolding.
Prove recursion equations (`f (n+1) = …`) and rewrite with them instead of evaluating `f 1000` by `rfl`.
example: (kernel) deep recursion detected

title: ring failed
explanation: The goal is not an identity of commutative (semi)rings as written, often because of ℕ subtraction or division, a hidden definition, or an inequality instead of an equation. `ring` then falls back to `ring_nf` and shows the normal form.
fixes: Compare the two normal forms that `ring_nf` displays to see which term differs.
Eliminate truncated subtraction/division first (`Nat.cast_sub`, `obtain ⟨k, rfl⟩ := Nat.exists_eq_add_of_le h`), or move to ℤ/ℝ with `zify`/`push_cast`.
For fields use `field_simp` then `ring`; for goals with hypotheses use `linear_combination h`.
example: ring failed, ring_nf subsidiary goal

title: norm_num failed to simplify
explanation: `norm_num` could not close or simplify the goal. It evaluates numerals and decides arithmetic facts like `Nat.Prime 1291`, but it does not know your definitions.
fixes: Pass the definitions and lemmas: `norm_num [f, Finset.sum_range_succ]`.
For finite checks over variables use `interval_cases x <;> norm_num`, or `decide`.
If the goal contains a variable, `norm_num` can only simplify; finish with `omega`, `linarith` or `positivity`.
example: norm_num failed to simplify

pattern: failed to prove positivity|not a positivity goal|positivity failed
title: positivity failed
explanation: `positivity` proves only goals of the form `0 < e`, `0 ≤ e` or `e ≠ 0` by syntactic structure. It fails on subtraction (`a - b`), on atoms without a sign hypothesis it can find, or on goals like `a < b`.
fixes: Rewrite the goal as `0 < b - a` (`sub_pos.mpr`) and prove it with `linarith`/`nlinarith`.
Supply facts about atoms by `have ha : 0 < a := …` first; positivity uses hypotheses only for atoms.
For ℕ subtraction, use `Nat.sub_pos_of_lt` or `omega`.
example: failed to prove positivity: the expression a - b is not positive

pattern: exact\?.?\s*could not close the goal|apply\? didn't find any relevant lemmas
title: exact? found nothing
explanation: Library search did not find a single lemma closing the goal. Search tactics are fine locally, but they must not stay in a nosorry submission.
fixes: Reformulate the goal into a standard form (`simp only` first, `push_neg`, move casts), then retry `exact?` or `apply?` locally.
Search by name pattern: Mathlib names follow the statement (`Finset.card_le_card`, `Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le`), and `rw?`/`simp?` can help.
Replace every `exact?` by the term it suggested before submitting.
example: `exact?` could not close the goal. Try `apply?` to see partial suggestions.

pattern: failed to prove termination|structural recursion cannot be used|fail to show termination
title: Termination proof failed
explanation: A recursive definition is not structurally recursive, and Lean could not prove that the well-founded measure decreases.
fixes: Add `termination_by n - i` (or another measure) and a `decreasing_by` block, proving the decrease with `omega` or `simp_wf; omega`.
Reformulate with structural recursion on `ℕ` or with `Nat.iterate`/`List.foldl`. Such definitions are also easier to `decide`.
`partial def` is refused on nosorry, so you need a real termination proof.
example: fail to show termination for f with errors: failed to prove termination

title: Unknown tactic
explanation: The tactic name is not available: missing `import Mathlib`, a Lean 3 tactic name (`norm_num1` variants, `by_contradiction`, `cases'` used wrongly), or a tactic renamed in recent Mathlib (`push_neg` vs `push Not`).
fixes: Make sure the file imports Mathlib (the challenge header does).
Use Lean 4 names: `by_contra`, `rcases`/`obtain`, `exact_mod_cast`, `field_simp`, `positivity`, `omega`, `decide`.
example: unknown tactic
